sysd-scale-059.title: Scalability: taking on more work without losing performance
sysd-scale-059.text:
A package delivery system scales by adding vehicles. But if every package must pass through a single warehouse for sorting, that warehouse limits how far the system can scale.

Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work. A system is scalable when it can take on more work, typically by adding resources, without losing performance. A search engine is a computing example: it must support growing numbers of users and growing numbers of indexed topics. Marc Brooker offers a precise test. A system is scalable in the range where the marginal cost of additional workload is nearly constant.

Design decides which side of that line a system lands on. Early Gnutella flooded every query to all nodes, so each peer's load grew with the number of peers. BitTorrent scales well because each peer's demand is independent of the number of peers. Strategy matters too. A system must keep applying a cost-effective way of scaling, and past the point where that strategy stops being financially viable, it is hard to scale further. A scalable database can be upgraded with more processors, devices and storage to process more transactions, easily and without shutting down.

sysd-scale-068.title: High availability: staying up when parts fail
sysd-scale-068.text:
Ask whether a system is available and the user's test is simple: can I reach it to submit, update or retrieve my work? If not, the system is unavailable from the user's perspective. High availability is a characteristic of a system that aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance, usually uptime, for a higher than normal period.

Reliability engineering offers three design principles: eliminate single points of failure, provide reliable crossover, and detect failures as they occur. {{ref:sysd-scale-056}} takes up the first. Eliminating them means building in {{ref:sysd-scale-073}}, so the failure of one component does not mean the failure of the entire system. Yet the crossover, where work passes from a failed part to its spare, tends to become the one part whose failure stops everything. So it must itself be reliable.

More parts are not automatically better. Complex systems have more potential failure points, which can undermine availability. But one simple machine must be taken down entirely for patching and operating system upgrades. Advanced designs use load balancing and {{ref:sysd-scale-058}} instead. The most common cause of outages is human error, so a highly available complex system must need less human intervention to restore operation.

A reliable system is available, but an available system is not necessarily reliable. A fault-tolerant system goes further. It has no service interruption, at a significantly higher cost. It needs a full duplicate of the hardware, so a second system takes over with no loss in uptime. A highly available system has minimal interruption instead.

sysd-scale-073.title: Redundancy: spare parts that raise availability
sysd-scale-073.text: Ten hosts that are each up only half the time can together reach 99.9023% availability. That is the promise of redundancy. It is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system to raise its reliability, usually as a standby or fail-safe. For N parallel components of availability X, combined availability is 1 - (1 - X)^N, so redundancy raises it exponentially. Passive redundancy uses excess capacity to reduce the impact of failures, accepting some performance decline. Active redundancy runs multiple items of the same kind and monitors them. Voting logic reconfigures around a failed item automatically, so performance does not decline. With an odd number of three or more devices doing identical work, the majority overrides any device that disagrees. The formula holds only if failures are independent and can be detected: two power supplies on one socket fail together. Redundancy also adds complexity, so Marc Brooker advises ensuring a net-positive gain.

sysd-scale-133.title: Mean time between failures: an average that misleads
sysd-scale-133.text: Most engineers assume a system has a 50% chance of surviving to its mean time between failures. It does not. The real chance is about 37%, and the misreading can lead to bad design decisions. Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation. For a non-repairable system the equivalent is mean time to failure. Three identical systems that fail after 100, 120 and 130 hours have an MTBF of 116.667 hours, the average of the three. The 37% follows from assuming a constant failure rate, of which MTBF is the reciprocal. Parts in series fail the system if any one fails, so adding them lowers the MTBF. Parts in parallel fail it only if the second fails during repair of the first, so faster repair shrinks the vulnerability window. For disk drives, the annualized failure rate is usually more relevant, because MTBF is only a mean lifetime.

sysd-scale-061.title: Scaling up or scaling out: one big machine or many
sysd-scale-061.text:
Large social networks exceed the capacity of even the largest supercomputer, so no single machine can carry them. That is one reason systems can grow in two directions. Scaling horizontally, or out, means adding nodes, such as going from one web server to three. Scaling vertically, or up, means adding resources such as CPUs, memory or storage to a single node. The reverse moves are scaling in and scaling down.

Vertical scaling adds power to an existing machine. It is simple to implement, easier to manage and data consistent. It also avoids the harder programming, and the throughput, latency and synchronization issues, of spreading work across nodes. The risks are high downtime, harder upgrades, and a single machine whose failure stops everything, as {{ref:sysd-scale-056}} explains. Some applications do not scale horizontally at all.

Horizontal scaling adds more instances to the pool, so load is distributed more evenly. It brings more redundancy, better tolerance of faults, flexibility, efficiency and easier upgrades. It also lets high-performance computing do tasks that once needed expensive supercomputers. The costs are increased complexity, data inconsistency and increased load on downstream services, plus software for efficient resource management and maintenance.

sysd-scale-138.title: Stateless and stateful: does the server remember you?
sysd-scale-138.text: An HTTP server understands each request on its own, as if it had never met you before. That is what makes a protocol stateless: the receiver keeps no session state from earlier requests, while a stateful protocol may retain it. IP and HTTP are stateless. TCP and FTP are stateful, and an FTP server keeps the user's login, working directory and transfer mode. Stateless designs buy visibility, reliability and scalability. Observing an exchange needs only one request, recovery from failures such as packet loss is easier, and the server can quickly free resources. The cost is performance, because repetitive data travels with every request. HTTP servers add state back with a session identifier in a cookie that refers to session state stored on the server. Stateless web servers can be autoscaled, as {{ref:sysd-q-067}} describes. On {{ref:sysd-reliab-050}}, scaling a stateless application only means adding pods, but stateful workloads are harder because their state must survive a pod restart.

sysd-scale-136.title: Amdahl's law: why more processors give less
sysd-scale-136.text: Speed up a part of a program that takes 10% of its running time by a factor of 10,000, and the whole program runs only 11% faster. That is Amdahl's law, a formula that limits the speedup of a task as resources are added to the system executing it. The overall gain is capped by the fraction of time the improved part is used. In parallel computing, the work that cannot run in parallel sets the limit, such as building a file list before threads process the files. Optimize a section that takes 99% of the time by a factor of 100 and the overall speedup is only 50. Half the potential gain is lost to the remaining 1%. So improve the part that takes most time. Take parts of 3 s and 1 s. Making the 3 s part twice as fast gives 1.60 overall, but making the 1 s part five times faster gives only 1.25. In a fixed-size computation, each added processor adds less usable power than the last.

sysd-q-067.title: Autoscaling: letting the load add and remove servers
sysd-q-067.text: Cloud providers charge for usage, not peak capacity, so a farm that always matches its load can lower its bills. Autoscaling is a cloud computing method that automatically adjusts the number of active servers in a server farm to match the load on the farm. It launches servers when activity is high and removes them when it is low. Because it follows actual usage instead of a fixed schedule, it handles unexpected spikes better. An autoscaling group is the set of instances under its control, with a desired capacity never below the minimum size or above the maximum. A scaling policy changes that capacity when a metric such as CPU utilization crosses a threshold. A cooldown period then blocks further scaling right after an action. Autoscaling is reactive by default. Scheduled scaling changes limits at set times for known, sudden changes. Netflix found that aggressive scaling up with delayed, cautious scaling down served uptime and responsiveness best.

sysd-scale-060.title: Dimensions of scalability: growth in six directions
sysd-scale-060.text: Growth is not one thing. Scalability can be measured along several dimensions, and each asks a different question. Administrative scalability is the ability of a growing number of organizations or users to access a system. Geographic scalability is staying effective while expanding from a local area to a larger region. Functional scalability adds new functionality without disrupting existing activities. Load scalability lets a distributed system expand and contract for heavier or lighter loads. Generation scalability means adopting new generations of components, and heterogeneous scalability means adopting components from different vendors.

sysd-scale-065.title: Diminishing returns: why doubling hardware falls short
sysd-scale-065.text: Doubling a machine's processors sounds like doubling its speed. Suppose 70% of a program can be parallelized and the computing power doubles from 4 processors to 8. The program speeds up by only roughly one-fifth, while a fully parallelizable problem would speed up twofold. Amdahl's law bounds the maximum speedup from P processors using α, the sequential fraction of a calculation, because only the remaining 1−α can be parallelized. Designers are often advised to favor hardware scalability over per-node capacity, since adding a node is typically cheaper than performance tuning. Even so, adding more hardware is not necessarily the optimal approach, because it has diminishing returns.

sysd-scale-066.title: The Universal Scalability Law and the limit of capacity
sysd-scale-066.text: At what point does adding capacity stop helping? Neil J. Gunther coined the Universal Scalability Law to answer that by calculation. It models the scalability of a distributed system using contention, the delay from waiting or queueing for shared resources, and coherency, the delay for data to become consistent. High contention indicates sequential processing that could be parallelized. High coherency suggests excessive dependencies among processes, so interactions should be minimized. The law lets you calculate in advance the maximum effective capacity of a system, and scaling up beyond that point is a waste.

sysd-scale-062.title: Eight strategies for scaling a system
sysd-scale-062.text: Engineers reach for eight common strategies when a system must scale. Stateless services do not rely on server-specific data, so they are easier to scale. Horizontal scaling adds more servers so the workload can be shared, and a load balancer spreads incoming requests evenly across them. Auto scaling policies adjust resources based on real-time traffic. Caching reduces the load on the database and handles repetitive requests at scale. Copying data across multiple nodes, taken up in {{ref:sysd-scale-043}}, scales reads while improving redundancy. Sharding, taken up in {{ref:sysd-scale-087}}, distributes data across multiple instances to scale writes as well as reads. Async processing moves time-consuming, resource-intensive tasks to background workers, and event-driven processing handles long-running tasks asynchronously, so the system can accept new requests.

sysd-scale-064.title: Scaling a database: indexes, caches, replicas and shards
sysd-scale-064.text: A slow database has more fixes than a bigger server. Check the application's query patterns and create the right indexes, then pre-compute complex query results in materialized views to read them faster. Denormalization reduces complex joins to improve query performance. Caching frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer reduces database load. Database scalability is the ability of a database system to perform additional work when given greater hardware resources, such as more servers, processors, memory and storage. Vertical scaling boosts the database server with more CPU, RAM or storage. Replicas of the primary database on other servers scale reads. Sharding splits tables into smaller pieces spread across servers and scales writes as well as reads. Algorithmic innovations include row-level locking and table and index partitioning. Architectural ones include shared-nothing and shared-everything designs for multi-server configurations.

sysd-scale-075.title: Computer clusters: many machines acting as one
sysd-scale-075.text: Ideally a cluster functions as a single system that users cannot tell from one machine. A computer cluster is a group of two or more computers, or nodes, that run in parallel to achieve a common goal. It distributes the workloads of many parallelizable tasks among its nodes, so they use the combined memory and processing power of every computer. A network connects the nodes, and software joins them into a cluster that may have shared storage, local storage on each node, or both. Typically at least one node is the leader node and entry point. It delegates incoming work to other nodes and, if needed, aggregates results into a response for the user. Clusters come in three types: highly available or fail-over, load balancing, and high-performance computing. The price is complexity. Every node needs the operating system, application and dependencies installed and updated, and shared storage and distributed data must be kept safe and in sync.

openers.scale: The more people use a system, the more work it has to do. Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work, and this part of the course begins with it. Beside it stands high availability, which aims to keep a system performing at an agreed level, usually uptime, for longer than normal. The tools range from adding nodes, or adding resources to a single node, to duplicating critical components as redundancy, to letting servers come and go automatically with the load. Each tool has limits, because a formula such as Amdahl's law caps how far a task can speed up as resources are added.
openers.scalability-and-availability: Two questions run through this chapter: how does a system grow, and how does it stay up? The answers start with two definitions. Scalability is the capacity to handle a growing amount of work, and high availability aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance for a higher than normal period. From there the chapter covers the strategies for scaling, the limits that Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law place on them, and the redundancy that keeps a system running when parts fail. It also shows how to measure reliability, starting with the mean time between failures, the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation.
